title: The Indian Ateliers Stitching Dior, Prada and Gucci's Finest Pieces
excerpt: Mumbai's Chanakya International employs 2,500 artisans for 30-plus luxury houses — but a row over Fendi's $10,000 Baguette has put the question of credit centre stage.
body:
• Mumbai-based Chanakya International employs some 2,500 artisans — from families spanning up to 13 generations — hand-embroidering pieces for more than 30 of the world's top luxury houses.
  • Its clients include Dior, Prada, Gucci, Schiaparelli and Fendi; for Dior's Fall 2023 show, 1,008 artisans created a monumental textile installation.
  • A row over Fendi's $10,000 mirror-and-bead Baguette, embroidered in Mumbai but sold under an Italian label, has put the question of credit and provenance centre stage.
  • Founder Vinod Shah's 1984 workshop has grown into a global creative force, with its own craft school and artworks shown at the Venice Biennale and the Vatican Library.

Some of the most intricate handwork in global luxury fashion is not made in Paris or Milan. It is made in Mumbai, by artisans whose families have practised the craft for as many as 13 generations — and whose names rarely appear on the labels. A new wave of reporting, led by a Guardian feature this week headlined "What we have is unique," is finally pulling the curtain back on the Indian ateliers stitching the world's finest pieces.

The house that Vinod Shah built

At the centre of the story is Chanakya International, founded in Mumbai in 1984 by Vinod Shah, a Gujarati entrepreneur who saw that European couture houses needed the hand-embroidery skills India had refined over centuries. Four decades on, the company works with more than 30 major luxury houses and employs roughly 2,400 to 2,500 artisans — a workforce that includes some of the finest zardozi, chikankari and bead-work hands in the world.

The business is now led by Shah's daughter, Karishma Swali, who has been its managing director and creative director for more than 30 years. Under her leadership, Chanakya founded the Chanakya School of Craft to train new generations of embroiderers, and its textile artworks have been exhibited at the Venice Biennale and the Vatican Library — a remarkable journey from subcontractor to cultural institution.

From Mumbai to the runway

The scale of the operation becomes clear at fashion week. For Dior's Fall 2023 show, a team of 1,008 Chanakya artisans produced a vast textile artwork — part toran, part tapestry — that formed the backdrop of the presentation. Dior, Prada, Gucci and Schiaparelli are all counted among the company's clients, and the Wall Street Journal recently profiled the Shah family as "the Mumbai family behind almost all the top luxury houses." CNBC TV18, marking the company's 40th year, traced its journey from a small embroidery unit to what it called a global creative force.

For the artisans, the work is as much art as labour. Techniques passed down through families — some spanning 13 generations — produce the mirror work, beadwork and thread embroidery that define couture's most photographed moments. Yet the finished garments typically carry only the European maison's name.

"What we have is unique."

— The Guardian, on India's luxury ateliers, September 2026

The credit question

That anonymity exploded into controversy this year over Fendi's Baguette. The bag — priced at $10,000 — featured 39,500 beads and 475 mirrors, requiring some 138 hours of handwork. The embroidery was executed by Chanakya's artisans in Mumbai; the bag was assembled in Italy and sold as Fendi.

Indian industrialist Harsh Goenka and Biocon founder Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw were among those who publicly questioned why the Indian hands behind the piece received no credit, igniting a debate about provenance, "made in" claims, and who profits from craft. Goenka later clarified his remarks, but the underlying question has not gone away: when a bag's defining labour happens in Mumbai, what does an Italian label actually mean?

The issue is not new — luxury houses have long sourced embroidery from India while keeping ateliers discreet — but the scrutiny is. As consumers increasingly ask where and by whom their clothes are made, the industry's Mumbai connection is becoming harder to keep in the footnotes.

Why it matters now

For India, the stakes go beyond fashion. Hand-embroidery is one of the country's great living traditions, employing hundreds of thousands of artisans, many of them women. The Chanakya model — formal employment, a dedicated school, and artworks that travel to the Biennale — offers one answer to how craft survives in a machine age: not as nostalgia, but as the irreplaceable core of the world's most expensive objects.

The next step, campaigners argue, is attribution — putting the atelier's name alongside the maison's. "What we have is unique" was the Guardian's headline. Whether the luxury world is ready to say it on the label is the question the next decade will answer.
nri_angle: For the Indian diaspora, the story reframes luxury shopping — the handwork behind a Dior or Fendi piece may well come from a Mumbai atelier, and credit for it is finally being claimed.
author: Diaspora Desk
